title: Bob and Ray
identity_notes: Bob Elliott and Ray Goulding’s long-running deadpan comedy/satire partnership. The historical broadcasts combined ad-libbed talk, sketches, mock interviews, serial parodies, characters, music and fake/real commercials across local, network and public radio. GRH’s current 1,837 playable objects are predominantly track-level compilation segments rather than one-to-one broadcast episodes, so broadcast metadata is never inferred merely from track order.

eras.label: WHDH Boston era
eras.notes: Breakfast/pregame improvisation and Matinee with Bob and Ray; local forms changed within this era.

eras.label: NBC network era
eras.notes: Daily network comedy with multiple short/long formats plus Inside Bob and Ray.

eras.label: NBC Monitor participation
eras.notes: Frequent short comedy appearances during Monitor’s first four years alongside other daily work.

eras.label: CBS daily era
eras.notes: 15-minute weekday network series; GRH compilation includes explicitly dated CBS tracks.

eras.label: New York local-radio era
eras.notes: Work across WINS, WOR and WHN; GRH collection explicitly includes a November 1962 WHN track and WOR last-show material dated April 30, 1976.

eras.label: Public-radio final era
eras.notes: Radio Hall of Fame gives 1982-1987; another encyclopedia uses a broader 1983-1990 span.

historical_context.title: Postwar radio culture as material for satire
historical_context.description: Bob and Ray emerged from postwar local radio and made the conventions of announcers, serials, interviews, giveaways and network presentation the raw material of their comedy.

historical_context.title: Advertising culture and Bob and Ray’s mock commercials
historical_context.description: Their fake commercials ran alongside legitimate sponsors; the advertising community embraced the satire and the duo also performed commercial voice work.

historical_context.title: Bob and Ray across the network-radio/television transition
historical_context.description: They moved into NBC network radio while also working in television, Monitor and later Mutual/CBS during the restructuring of network radio in the 1950s.
